_: THE SWEEP THAT SAYS THE SECONDS ARE COUNTED AND NOT DECORATION — run it
from the repository root:
cargo run -q --manifest-path tools/injection-harness/Cargo.toml -- \
tools/twice-compiled/injection-sweep.json
Round 1092 built this census over counts and its report ranked the repair by
rows. This round priced every row, and a price is easier to get wrong than a
count in a way no total shows: the two halves still add up, the percentages
still print, and only the ORDER of the list is a lie. Each injection below
removes one mechanism — the window, the direction each figure errs in, the
seconds of a job's own repeats, the law against a census with no clocks in
it — and names the test that must go red for it.
The last seven are of the OTHER kind. Everything above breaks a reading of
records that already exist; those break `main.rs`, which is BOTH ways into
this gate and had no test of any kind because nothing here ran the binary.
Five break the replay — not applying the variables it owns, running every job
in one tree, writing every job's records to one file, running the steps that
install what this machine has, and letting a failed step end the run — and
two break the runner entrance, where the workflow is read off the runner and
the gate's own half-built job is left out of its own census. Every one of the
seven was unreadable before `tests/entrances.rs`.
Scoped to this crate's own suite. The reading tests build nothing; the four
replay tests compile one dependency-free crate in a worktree apiece and the
two runner tests compile nothing at all, so the whole sweep is still seconds.

injections.name: the-window-is-the-first-line-to-the-last
injections.why: records are appended when a compiler EXITS and cargo runs as many as the machine has cores, so the earliest start routinely arrives last; a window read off the order of the lines is short every time, and a job that looks busier than it was is a job whose duplication looks cheaper to remove than it is

injections.name: a-job-is-busy-for-the-sum-of-its-compilers
injections.why: cargo runs as many compilers as the machine has cores, so summing their durations reports a job busy for longer than the clock allows and leaves it with no idle time at all — and idle time is exactly the part of a window that removing compilations cannot shorten

injections.name: the-estimate-scales-the-whole-window
injections.why: this is the assumption the round refused to carry: scaling a job's whole window by the work removed treats the minutes it spends running what it just built as though they compiled, and the two jobs in this repository with the most to share are the two that spend the longest running what they built — the estimate would promise a merged job shorter than either of the two it replaces

injections.name: the-surviving-compilation-is-priced-at-the-cheapest
injections.why: the same unit takes different times in different jobs and the one compilation that survives a repair has to be priced at one of them — taking the cheapest makes the floor as low as the evidence allows and every saving reported as large as it can be, which is a gate arguing for the repair rather than measuring it

injections.name: a-merge-is-credited-with-the-dearer-of-the-two
injections.why: the same error one step further on, from the other side: merging removes ONE of the two compilations of a shared unit, and crediting the merge with the dearer one reports a saving larger than the least it can win — the number this report exists to keep somebody from overstating

injections.name: a-jobs-own-repeats-cost-nothing
injections.why: the half of the surplus merging CANNOT reach is a job compiling one unit twice over its own separate workspaces, and pricing it at zero moves those seconds into the cross-job half by arithmetic — the report then recommends merging for minutes that merging cannot win

injections.name: the-crate-breakdown-is-counted-and-not-priced
injections.why: this is the whole finding of the round: ranked by rows the head of the duplication is `build_script_build`, and a breakdown that carries counts with the seconds left at zero prints that ranking as though it were the price — the repair goes where the rows are and the money stays where it was

injections.name: a-census-of-no-jobs-reads-as-clean
injections.why: this is not hypothetical: a local replay refused all nine jobs of the workflow, and the census printed `0 compilations across 0 job(s)`, every total a clean zero, and signed off with `every one of the 0 job(s) recorded what it compiled` — a measurement that never happened wearing the exact shape of a file in good order

injections.name: a-job-is-skipped-for-a-variable-the-replay-replaces
injections.why: every job in this workflow carries `MNEMOSYNE_RUSTC_LOG: ${{ github.workspace }}/…`, which the replay overwrites before running a step; reading it as an expression only GitHub can resolve refuses all nine jobs over a value nobody reads, which is what closed the replay entrance the day the recorder was wired in

injections.name: the-replay-replays-the-gate-itself
injections.why: the gate's job downloads what the others wrote and joins it, so replaying it reads a directory the replay is still filling and puts the instrument's own build into its own reading — the mistake this crate already corrects once, for the log the gate writes on a runner

injections.name: a-census-with-no-clocks-in-it-is-accepted
injections.why: a job running an older recorder leaves a log whose counts are all present and whose seconds are all zero — every total adds up, and the report says the work is free, which is the finding that would argue for merging every job in the file

injections.name: the-replay-does-not-set-the-variables-it-owns
injections.why: the replay overwrites `RUSTC_WRAPPER` and `MNEMOSYNE_RUSTC_LOG` for every step it runs, because the workflow spells both as GitHub expressions; a step run without them either records nothing or records into whatever the caller's environment named, and both leave a job's log absent — which is the same output as a job with nothing to build

injections.name: every-job-replays-into-the-same-tree
injections.why: a worktree per job is what makes each job's build COLD, and a cold build is the only one a wrapper can see: cargo runs no compiler for a unit that is already fresh. Replaying every job in one tree leaves the first job with a census and every job after it with an empty log, so the duplication this gate exists to count disappears into what looks like jobs that compile nothing

injections.name: every-job-records-into-one-file
injections.why: the census reads a job's name off the file its records are in, so a replay writing every job to one path produces one blob wearing the shape of a census — every unit in it, no two jobs sharing anything, and a clean zero for the duplication. `Refusal::LogIsNotNamedForItsJob` is the same mistake caught in the WORKFLOW's wiring; nothing was watching the replay's own

injections.name: every-job-resolves-head-for-itself
injections.why: `HEAD` is a name for whatever the repository is on and a replay takes hours, so reading it per job is how a census comes to be of two source trees at once — which happened here: four jobs from one commit and the fifth from another that landed mid-run, with nothing in the report saying so. The numbers survived only because that commit touched no manifest

injections.name: the-replay-installs-what-this-machine-already-has
injections.why: a replay runs a job's steps verbatim EXCEPT two named prefixes, and `rustup` is one of them: a hosted runner installs a toolchain this machine already has, and running that step would change the compiler under the very measurement being taken — the units would then be shared with nothing and the census would report a repository with no duplication in it

injections.name: a-step-that-failed-ends-the-replay
injections.why: the compilations a failing step paid for are already in the log and the census is of what CI PAID FOR, so a failure is named and the replay carries on. Making it fatal throws away every job after the first gate that goes red — and the jobs of this workflow are gates, so a replay would be abandoned by the ordinary case rather than the exceptional one

injections.name: the-gate-counts-its-own-half-built-job
injections.why: on a runner this gate reads a directory of logs while its OWN job is still building, so its own log cannot be there yet; counting it makes the gate refuse the very push it is part of, every time, for a job that did nothing wrong. The control is the test that removes `$GITHUB_JOB` entirely and requires exactly that refusal — so the pair says the drop is load-bearing rather than tidy

injections.name: the-workflow-reference-is-read-whole
injections.why: `$GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF` is `owner/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@refs/heads/main`, and the census is of ONE workflow read out of the middle of it. Taking the reference whole points the gate at a path that does not exist in the checkout, which is how a gate ends up judging a file nobody has
